note: Pet-toxicity is the flagship safety feature of Cuttings Garden and runs fully offline. Facts are our own summaries built from the ASPCA Toxic and Non-Toxic Plants reference (facts are not copyrightable; page text was not copied). toxicToSmallPets covers rabbits/rodents and is null where reliable data was not found. Any entry we could not confirm carries "verify": true and should be double-checked before relying on it.

entries.severityNote: Insoluble calcium oxalates cause intense oral burning, drooling, and vomiting if chewed.
Insoluble calcium oxalates; oral irritation, drooling, and difficulty swallowing.
Insoluble calcium oxalates; oral irritation, drooling, vomiting. Common cause of pet ER visits.

Non-toxic. Cats may still vomit if they eat a large amount of the foliage.
Triterpenoid saponins; foliage is more toxic than the berries. Vomiting, diarrhea, drooling.
Widely regarded as non-toxic to cats and dogs, but it is not individually listed by ASPCA.

entries.severityNote: Contains linalool; mild nausea and lethargy, worse with concentrated oils. Small-pet data not confirmed.
SERIOUS: allium compounds damage red blood cells and can cause anemia. Vomiting, weakness, and dark urine. Cats are especially sensitive. Applies to all onions, garlic, chives, and leeks.
entries.source: ASPCA Toxic and Non-Toxic Plants (Allium species)

The ripe fruit is safe, but the foliage is a nightshade and is best kept away from pets. Pet-safety of the plant is not firmly established; verify before relying on this.

entries.severityNote: Green foliage, stems, and unripe fruit contain solanine; GI upset, lethargy, and weakness. The ripe red fruit itself is safe.
